newsitem.title: UK: Scientists attack UK government for madcow delays.
newsitem.headline: Scientists attack UK government for madcow delays.

text.p: British scientists attacked the government and the meat industry on Friday for delays, negligence and a lack of funding they say helped extend the mad cow epidemic.

Reaction to the epidemic was slow and the government failed to heed several warnings about the dangers, Gerald Collee, a microbiologist at Edinburgh University Medical School and Ray Bradley of the Central Veterinary Laboratory said.
But, they added in a report for the Lancet medical journal, regulations currently in place to make sure British beef and milk are safe should be enough to protect people from infection.

"Delayed opportunities for tighter controls together with slippage and manifestly careless, and, from time to time, dishonest practices have been responsible for thnce of almost 30,000 after-the-ban cases to date," they wrote.
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) reached epidemic proportions in Britain in the 1980s and still lingers on, although experts predict it will be gone by 2005.

The government denied there was any danger to people until last March, when scientists said a new variety of the human version of BSE, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), was probably due to people eating infected meat.
Rules had been phased in preventing the use of specified bovine offal (SBO) -- cattle parts found to carry infection including the brain, spinal cord, intestine and lymph tissue.

Last year the government banned using meat from cattle over 30 months old and started a cull of those believed most likely to develop BSE -- aimed mostly at ending a European Union ban on exports of British beef.
There is also a ban on the probable source of BSE --- feed made from the remains of sheep, which can be infected with scrapie, their own version of the brain disease.
But, Collee and Bradley said, "there has been some slippage in our control measures".

"There has been concern that carelessness, negligence, evasion and fraud frustrated the legislaey wrote. "About 80 percent of all cases of BSE reported in November and December 1996 are in cattle born after the feed ban."
There were severe failures in regard to animal health, they said. "Only about half the theoretical tonnage of SBO was properly separated and rendered (by July 1994)," they wrote.
Export controls were slow and steps not taken quickly enough to make sure other animal feed did not contaminate, or get contaminated by, cattle feed.

"The authorities were slow to realise that only a small amount of infected brain material was an effective oral dose," they added. Therefore, controls aimed at keeping brains out of minced beef products went into effect too slowly.
Expert advice to set up a committee on animal feed was accepted but then ignored and resources were not diverted to get a quick test for BSE developed. There still is no fast test.
The latest animal recorded with BSE was born in autumn 1993, "well after the feed and SBO bans were in place," they said.
Finally, a lack of funding of science over the past 20 years meant it took too long for scientists to get up and running on the emergency, they said.
They repeated estimates that there would be 6,950 cases of BSE between 1997 and 2001 if there was no culling or premature slaughter and if infected feed had truly been eliminated.
